<reason>Side A (CON) won on execution and flow despite Side B's more memorable framing. A answered both pressure questions squarely with substantive content: an enforceable framework (written reasons, notice, review, proof of substantial loss, less restrictive measures) and an operational product-vs-seller criterion that distinguished the racial-discrimination analogy. That criterion was never rebutted by B, and A's textual overreach point — the motion names processors and app stores generally, with no dominance or boutique exception — went unanswered except by B's interpretive stretch that curation 'is its product' rather than reputational fear. B's 'ban with paperwork' closing rejoin was strong, and the chokepoint/prejudice-relay case was morally powerful, but B suffered real execution costs: three of five turns were clipped for exceeding word limits, the boutique concession undercuts the categorical motion, and B's rebuttal-2 claim that CON 'never named one' enforceable duty mischaracterized the exchange since A then produced those duties. A's closing crystallized the divergence cleanly: the sides differ only when substantiated, unavoidable losses exist, and PRO refuses to weigh that harm at all.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's closing reframe of Side A's review framework — 'written reasons, notice, review — and then, at the end of the process, the same ban, now with paperwork' — was the sharpest single exchange, but Side A's rebuttal 2 (A4.1–A4.4) was the most decisive: it supplied the enforceable duties B demanded, offered the product-vs-seller criterion against the discrimination analogy, and turned B's own boutique concession into proof of the motion's overreach.</best_rebuttal>
